quiz.p: Why did water go into a glass that was already full of dry chana?
opts: The gaps between the grains were full of air, and the water pushed it out
quiz.why: A full glass of grain is part grain and part air. Water can take the place of the air but not of the grains. Bubbles of air came up as it did.

quiz.p: Anu tries to blow up a balloon inside a closed, empty bottle. It hardly grows. Why?
opts: The bottle is full of air, and the air has nowhere to go
quiz.why: Air takes up space. The air already in the bottle stops the balloon growing. With a hole in the bottle, it blows up easily.

quiz.p: A syringe of air is blocked at the tip. Can you push the plunger in?
opts: Yes, part of the way, because air can be squashed
Yes, all the way to zero
quiz.why: Air can be compressed, so the plunger goes in part of the way. It cannot go to zero, because the squashed air pushes back harder and harder.

quiz.p: Why can air be squashed, but water hardly at all?
opts: Air particles are far apart. Water particles touch
quiz.why: There is space between air particles, so pushing moves them closer. Water particles already touch. Picking 'heavier' is a fair thought, but weight is not what stops water being squashed.

quiz.p: About how much does one litre of air weigh?
quiz.why: One litre of air weighs about 1.2 grams. One litre of water weighs about 1 kilogram, more than 800 times as much.

quiz.p: Which gas makes up most of the air?
quiz.why: About four-fifths of air is nitrogen. Oxygen is about one-fifth. Carbon dioxide is only a tiny part. Many people guess oxygen, because it is the one we need.

quiz.p: What do our cells need oxygen for?
opts: To make our hair grow longer
quiz.why: Cells use oxygen to get energy from the food we eat. Without it, they stop working in minutes.

quiz.p: Compared with the air around us, the air you breathe out has:
opts: more oxygen and less carbon dioxide
less oxygen and more carbon dioxide
quiz.why: Your cells used some oxygen and made carbon dioxide. Breathed-out air has about 16 parts oxygen in 100 instead of 21, and about 100 times more carbon dioxide.

quiz.p: In bright sunlight, what does a leaf take in from the air?
quiz.why: In light, leaves take in carbon dioxide through their stomata and use it with water to make sugar. They also use a little oxygen, but they give out much more than they use.

opts: Yes, every living part of a plant needs oxygen, day and night
quiz.why: Plants use oxygen all the time, in their leaves, stems and roots. In the day they also make oxygen, more than they use. That is why roots in flooded soil can die.

quiz.p: A lotus stem is full of holes. How do the holes help the lotus?
opts: They carry air down to the stem and roots stuck in airless mud
quiz.why: The mud at the bottom of a pond has almost no oxygen. The holes are air canals that carry air down from the leaves.

quiz.p: In ancient Greece, what did the squeezed wine bag and the water thief show?
opts: That a pot that looks empty is full of air
That water is heavier than wine
That air is made of fire
quiz.why: A squeezed bag full of air pushes back, and a covered water thief keeps water out. Both show air is a real thing that takes up space.

items.p: Meena, a girl in Class 3, fills a glass to the top with dry chana. Then she pours in water. What happens?
opts: The water spills over at once
A lot of water goes in, and bubbles come up
The chana floats out of the glass
items.why: The gaps between the grains are full of air. The water pushes the air out, so bubbles rise, and the water fills the gaps. A strong answer says where the water went: into the spaces the air had filled.

items.p: Arjun says, "An empty bottle has nothing in it." Describe a test that shows him he is wrong.
items.a: Push a balloon into the bottle and stretch its mouth over the neck. Try to blow it up. It hardly grows, because the bottle is full of air, and the air has nowhere to go.
items.why: A strong answer names a real test and says what you would see, and why it shows air is there.

items.p: Air has no weight.
items.why: False. One litre of air weighs about 1.2 grams. The air in a small bedroom weighs about 32 kilograms.

items.p: Squashing something into less space is called ____ it.
items.why: To compress means to squash into less space. Air can be compressed. Water hardly at all.

items.p: Match each gas to what it does.
pairs: our cells need it to get energy from food
we breathe out more of it, and plants use it to make food
makes up most of the air
water as a gas in the air
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These four gases are the ones that matter most in this unit. Knowing what each does explains breathing and plants.

items.p: Draw a glass full of chana. Use dots to show where the air is.
items.a: A glass with round chana grains, and dots in all the gaps between the grains, right down to the bottom.
items.why: A strong drawing puts air in every gap, not only at the top, because the bubbles came up from all through the glass.
items.art: An empty outline of a glass on a page.

items.p: Sort these things. Does each one have air hiding inside it, or not?
items.a: see items
items.why: Things with holes or gaps hold air. Solid metal and glass have no gaps for air. A strong sorter thinks about gaps, not about whether a thing is soft.

items.p: Why do we breathe in air?
opts: Our cells need its oxygen to get energy from food
items.why: Our cells use oxygen to get energy from food. Breathing brings oxygen in, and takes carbon dioxide out. The chest grows when we breathe, but that is because of the air, not the reason for breathing.

items.p: Lakshmi waters her tulsi plant every hour, so the soil is always soaking wet. After a week, the plant looks sick. Use what you know about air to explain why.
items.a: Roots need oxygen from the air in the soil. When the soil is always soaked, water fills all the air spaces, so the roots cannot get oxygen.
items.why: A strong answer says roots need oxygen and that water pushes the air out of the soil, as it did from the chana.

items.p: Plants take in oxygen only at night.
items.why: False. Plants use oxygen day and night. In sunlight they also make much more oxygen than they use, so they give oxygen out in the day.

items.p: Put these in order, from the first thing that happens when you breathe in, to the last.
items: Blood carries oxygen to your cells
Oxygen passes into your blood in the lungs
a: Oxygen passes into your blood in the lungs
Blood carries oxygen to your cells
items.why: Air goes in through the windpipe to the lungs. In the lungs, oxygen passes into the blood. The blood carries it all round the body.

items.p: Farhan blocks the tip of a syringe full of air and pushes the plunger. What happens?
opts: It does not move at all
It goes in part of the way, then springs back when he lets go
It goes in all the way and stays there
items.why: The air is squashed into less space, and pushes back. So the plunger goes in part of the way and springs back. Picking 'stays there' misses that squashed air pushes back.

items.p: The tiny holes on a leaf that let air in and out are called ____.
items.why: Stomata are tiny holes, mostly on the underside of leaves. Carbon dioxide goes in through them and oxygen comes out.

items.p: When Kavya breathes in deeply, the string round her chest gets longer. Why?
items.a: Her lungs fill with air, and air takes up space. Her ribs move out to make room, so her chest gets bigger.
items.why: A strong answer links the bigger chest to air taking up space.

items.p: Three people talk about the bubbles that came up when water was poured into a glass of chana.

views.says: The bubbles were air that was hiding between the grains.
The bubbles were gas coming out of the chana itself.
Maybe both. Most of the bubbles came from the gaps, but a few could come from inside the grains.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Give a reason from your own test. Then say what you would do to check another person's idea.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with evidence: most bubbles came at once, from between the grains, as the water reached them. To check Rohan's idea, put one chana grain in water and watch whether it gives bubbles by itself.
items.why: This is a real question. Dry grains do have a little air in tiny cracks, so Amma's view is fair. The test with a single grain can show how much comes from the grain itself.

items.p: A syringe full of air can be pushed in, but a syringe full of water hardly moves. Explain why, using the word particles.
items.a: In air, the particles are far apart, with empty space between them, so pushing moves them closer. In water, the particles already touch, so there is no room to push them into.
items.why: A strong answer compares the spacing of the particles in both, not only says air is 'soft'.

items.p: In the Full Glass test, Nila used big chana and tiny mustard seeds. Both glasses took in about the same amount of water. Why?
opts: Mustard seeds soak up water faster
Big grains leave big gaps but fewer of them. Small seeds leave small gaps but many more of them
The water was not poured carefully
items.why: The size of each gap changes, but so does the number of gaps. For round grains of one size, the share of air comes out about the same. Picking 'soak up faster' is a fair thought, but the seeds take in very little water in a few minutes.

items.p: One litre of air weighs about ____ grams.
items.why: One litre of air near the ground weighs about 1.2 grams, about as much as a paper clip.

items.p: The air you breathe out has no oxygen left in it.
items.why: False. Breathed-out air still has about 16 parts oxygen in 100, compared with 21 in the air around us. That is why rescue breathing can help someone.

items.p: A soda water bottle gets a few grams lighter after it goes flat. What does this show?
items.why: The fizz is carbon dioxide gas. When it escaped, the bottle lost its weight. So gases have weight.

items.p: Sort these. Is each one taken in or given out by a leaf in bright sunlight?
items.a: see items
items.why: In sunlight, a leaf takes in carbon dioxide and water, and makes sugar. Oxygen is left over and goes out. Some water also escapes as vapour through the stomata.

items.p: A lotus has their roots stuck in mud at the bottom of a pond. What problem does this give the lotus, and how do the holes in the stem help?
items.a: Mud under water has almost no air, so the roots and stem can't get oxygen there. The holes are air canals that carry air down from the leaves to the parts in the mud.
items.why: A strong answer says the problem first, no oxygen in mud, then how the canals solve it.

items.p: You cover the top of a straw with your finger and push it into a glass of water. What happens?
opts: Only a little water gets in, because the air inside is in the way
items.why: The air in the straw can't get out, so the water can't take its place. Lift your finger and the water rushes in.

items.p: Put these in order, from the lightest to the heaviest.
items: the air in a small bedroom
a: the air in a small bedroom
items.why: One litre of air is about 1.2 grams. One litre of water is about 1,000 grams. The air in a 3 by 3 by 3 metre bedroom is about 32,000 grams, or 32 kilograms.

items.p: Draw a plant in a pot in the daytime and at night. Use arrows to show which gases go in and which come out.
items.a: Day: carbon dioxide arrow going in, a big oxygen arrow coming out, and a small oxygen arrow going in. Night: only an oxygen arrow going in and a carbon dioxide arrow coming out.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that plants use oxygen day and night, and give out oxygen only when light lets them photosynthesise.
items.art: Two outlines of a potted plant side by side, one under a sun and one under a moon.

items.p: Anjali says, "A football full of air is heavier than a flat one." Shanthi says, "No, air has no weight." How could they find out who is right?
items.a: Weigh the flat football on a kitchen scale. Pump it up hard and weigh it again. If it is heavier, the extra air has weight. The difference is only a few grams, so the scale must show grams.
items.why: A strong answer describes a fair test with one change, and says what result would show each girl right.

items.p: Bubbles came out of a lump of dry soil under water. This shows that soil has air in it.
items.why: True. Soil has tiny gaps between its grains, and the gaps hold air. Water pushes the air out as it soaks in.

items.p: Match each thing to the way it uses compressed air.
pairs: stays firm so the wheel rolls
bounces back when it hits the ground
carries lots of air in a small space
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Compressed air pushes back, and lots of it fits in a small space. Each of these uses one of those facts.

items.p: A family is talking about keeping money plants in the children's bedroom.

views.says: Plants use up oxygen at night. Keep them out of the bedroom.
Plants give us oxygen, so a bedroom full of plants makes the air much fresher.
A few plants are fine, but they only change the air a tiny bit, either way.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Use facts from this unit. Then say one thing another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer sides with Sneha and gives reasons: plants do use oxygen at night, as Paati says, but very little, far less than one sleeping person. Plants do give out oxygen in light, as Revathi says, but a few plants hardly change the air of a whole room. An open window changes it far more.
items.why: Each person has part of the truth. A strong answer gives Paati and Revathi credit for the real facts behind their ideas.

items.p: Why do plant pots have holes in the bottom?
opts: So extra water drains away and air can get back into the soil
items.why: When extra water drains out, air comes back into the gaps in the soil. Roots need the oxygen in that air.

items.p: Long ago in ancient Greece, people argued about a pot with nothing you could see inside it.

views.says: The pot is empty. Air is nothing at all.
The pot is full of air. Squeeze an empty-looking wine bag, and it pushes back.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use your own tests to support your answer. Then say why the first idea seemed sensible to people.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Anaxagoras, with evidence: the balloon in the bottle, the straw water thief and the bubbles from the chana. It also says the first idea made sense because air can't be seen or smelt, and usually feels like nothing.
items.why: A strong answer gives evidence from the child's own tests, and is fair to the old idea by saying why people believed it.

items.p: Hero of Alexandria wrote that air is made of tiny pieces with empty space between them. Which of your tests supports this idea best? Explain.
items.a: The syringe test. Air could be squashed into less space, but water could not. If air is tiny pieces with gaps between them, pushing moves the pieces closer and closes the gaps.
items.why: A strong answer picks the syringe and explains how gaps between particles let air be squashed.

items.p: Priya pours water into a glass of dry moong until it is full. Then she tips the water out and measures it. She gets 80 ml. Her glass holds 200 ml. What share of the glass of moong was air?
items.why: 80 out of 200 is the same as 2 out of 5, or two-fifths. A strong answer checks: 2 fifths of 200 is 80.

items.p: If you squash the air in a syringe to half the space, the air weighs half as much.
items.why: False. The same air is still there, only packed closer. Its weight stays the same. Nothing was taken away.

items.p: Revathi poured water into a glass of sand and a glass of chana. The sand took in much less water than she expected, and some sand stayed dry on top. Suggest two reasons.
items.a: Wet sand clumps and can trap air, so the water cannot reach all the gaps. She might have poured too fast, so the water sat on top. Fine grains of different sizes also pack tighter, with small grains filling the gaps between big ones.
items.why: A strong answer thinks about how the test was done, not only about the sand. Spotting a weak test is part of being a scientist.

items.p: Why does a full bottle of water empty faster when you swirl it as you turn it over?
opts: The water spins and leaves an open path in the middle for air to get in
items.why: The water can only leave if air takes its place. A spinning funnel of water leaves a hole down the middle, so air flows in steadily instead of in glugs.

items.p: Put these steps of the Lift the Books challenge in the order they happen.
items: The bag swells and pushes on the books
You blow air into the straw
Air takes up space inside the bag
a: You blow air into the straw
Air takes up space inside the bag
The bag swells and pushes on the books
items.why: The air must go in and take up space before the bag can push the books up.

items.p: Most of the air we breathe in is nitrogen, but our body does not use it. So why do we breathe in so much nitrogen?
items.a: Because nitrogen is most of the air around us, about four-fifths. We cannot pick out only the oxygen, so we breathe in the whole mixture and breathe the nitrogen out again unchanged.
items.why: A strong answer says that air is a mixture and we take it all in, using only the part we need.

items.p: Mangrove trees at Pichavaram in Tamil Nadu grow in salty mud. Many send up roots that stick out of the mud like pencils. What do these roots do?
opts: Take in air at low tide and pass it down to the roots below
items.why: The mud has almost no air. These breathing roots take in air when the tide is out and carry it to the roots buried in the mud, which need oxygen to live.

items.p: Draw a zoom-in of the air inside a syringe before and after you push the plunger. Use dots for the particles.
items.a: Before: a few dots spread far apart in a long space. After: the same number of dots, closer together, in a shorter space.
items.why: A strong drawing keeps the same number of dots in both pictures, because no air was added or taken away.
items.art: Two empty syringe outlines, one long and one pushed in.

items.p: Early on, the Earth's air had almost no oxygen. Today about one-fifth of the air is oxygen. Where did it come from, and why does this matter to you?
items.a: It came from living things that photosynthesise: first tiny beings in the sea called cyanobacteria, later plants and plankton. It matters because every breath I take has oxygen that living things made.
items.why: A strong answer names living things as the source, and links it to the child's own breathing.

items.p: In the Full Glass test, Kavya forgot to fill her second glass of water to the same line each time. Why does that matter?
opts: She can't compare how far the water dropped, because each try started at a different level
items.why: Each try must start the same way, so that only the grain changes. Otherwise a bigger drop might come from a fuller glass, not from more air.

items.p: Plants make food from carbon dioxide and water using light. This is called ____.
items.why: Photosynthesis is how plants make sugar from carbon dioxide and water, using light. Oxygen is left over.

items.p: Label the parts of a lotus that help air reach the mud: leaf, leaf stalk, air canals, underground stem in the mud.
items.a: The leaf floats on top. The leaf stalk runs down from it through the water. The air canals are the hollow tubes inside the stalk and stem. The underground stem lies in the mud at the bottom.
items.why: Each part is on the path air takes from the open air down to the mud.
items.art: An unlabelled cut-away drawing of a lotus in a pond with four blank label lines.

items.p: A sealed plastic bottle with its cap on is hard to crush. An open one crushes easily. Explain why, using what you know about air.
items.a: In the sealed bottle the air can't get out. When you squeeze, the air gets squashed and pushes back. In the open bottle, the air just leaves through the neck.
items.why: A strong answer says the air in the sealed bottle has nowhere to go, so it pushes back.

applications: Cycle, scooter and car tyres are filled with compressed air, so they stay firm and soften the bumps.
Footballs, volleyballs and basketballs bounce because of the compressed air inside them.
Bubble wrap and air pillows in parcels protect things, because squashed air pushes back.
Divers, firefighters and hospital patients get air or oxygen from tanks, where a lot of it is squeezed into a small space.
Pressure cookers, pumps and the air brakes on buses and trucks all use the push of squashed or heated air and steam.
Doctors give rescue breathing because breathed-out air still has enough oxygen to help someone.
Gardeners make holes in pots and loosen soil so roots get air.
Rice farmers know their crop can grow in flooded fields because rice plants carry air down to their roots.
Houses are built with windows and ventilators so that stale air goes out and fresh air comes in.
Weather scientists measure the weight of the air above us, called air pressure, to forecast rain and storms.

open_questions.q: Exactly how much of the world's oxygen is made in the sea, and how much on land?
open_questions.why_open: Tiny sea beings are very hard to count across a whole ocean. Most estimates say about half, but the numbers keep changing as scientists measure more.

open_questions.q: Why did oxygen take so long to build up in the air after tiny sea beings started making it?
open_questions.why_open: Rocks show a gap of perhaps hundreds of millions of years. Scientists argue about what used up the oxygen first, such as iron in the sea and gases from volcanoes.

open_questions.q: How much does the air in our cities harm children's lungs over many years?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know that dirty air is harmful, but measuring exactly how much, for each kind of pollution, takes studies of many children over many years.

open_questions.q: How exactly do plant roots sense that the soil has too little air, and what do they do about it?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found some of the signals roots use, but the full story of how they sense and respond is still being worked out.

maths.problem: In the Full Glass test, Meenakshi used a 200 ml glass. Water poured in: chana 80 ml, moong 76 ml, mustard seeds 74 ml. Which grain left the most air? How much more than the least?
maths.answer: Chana left the most air. That is 6 ml more than the mustard seeds.
maths.explain: The biggest number is 80 ml, for chana. The smallest is 74 ml, for mustard seeds. 80 - 74 = 6 ml. 6 ml is small compared with 200 ml, so the three grains left almost the same amount of air.
maths.context: This is about the Full Glass test, where you pour water into a glass full of grain to find how much air was in the gaps. Here are some made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Taking one number from another tells you whether the difference between grains is big or tiny.

maths.problem: A glass holds 200 ml. When it is full of chana, 80 ml of water goes in. What fraction of the glass of chana was air? Give it in its simplest form.
maths.explain: 80 out of 200 is 80/200. Divide both numbers by 40: 2/5. Check: one-fifth of 200 is 40, so two-fifths is 80.
maths.context: This is about the Full Glass test with chana.
maths.why_maths: A fraction lets you compare glasses of different sizes, because it shows the share of air, not just the amount.

maths.problem: One cubic metre of air weighs about 1.2 kilograms. Arjun's bedroom is 4 metres long, 3 metres wide and 3 metres high. About how much does the air in it weigh?
maths.explain: The volume is 4 × 3 × 3 = 36 cubic metres. 36 × 1.2 = 36 + 7.2 = 43.2. So the air weighs about 43 kilograms, more than a 10-year-old child.
maths.context: This is about the project where you measure a room to work out how heavy its air is.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying turns three easy measurements into the weight of something you can never put on a scale.

maths.problem: Divya pushed a 10 ml syringe of air in to the 5 ml mark. Her mother pushed it to the 4 ml mark. Their grandmother pushed a 10 ml syringe of water and it moved less than half a ml. What pattern do you see, and what does it tell you?
maths.answer: The harder the push, the more the air squashed, but the water hardly squashed at all.
maths.explain: Divya halved the space of the air, from 10 to 5. Her mother, pushing harder, got it to 4. But even a strong push hardly moved the water. So air squashes more the harder you push, and water hardly squashes at all.
maths.context: This is about the syringe experiment, where you block the tip and push the plunger. Here are some made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the numbers side by side shows a pattern you can explain with particles.

roots.context: We have found out that air fills every gap, has weight, and keeps us and plants alive. Now we ask what air tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Your glass looked full of chana, yet over a third of a glass of water still went in. Tiny mustard seeds left about the same share of air as big chana. Smaller seeds leave smaller gaps, but many more of them. So a glass of round grains is about one-third air, whether the grains are big or small.
deep_truth.habit: We call a glass of grain 'full' when we can see no room left, and we expect big grains to leave much more empty space than small ones. Both habits come from what our eyes notice. The test shows the gaps are full of air, and that the share of air hardly depends on grain size.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Full Glass test, a glass filled to the line with chana, moong or mustard seeds still took in a lot of water, and bubbles of air came out as it did. The amounts for the three grains came out close, though the chana are several times bigger than the mustard seeds.

three.who_am_i: Every few seconds you take air into your body, and some of its oxygen becomes part of the way you live. You are not sealed off from the air. You are always sharing it.
three.what_is_life: Plants and tiny sea beings put oxygen into the air, and every breathing being uses it. Life made the air we breathe.
three.what_is_this_world: We live at the bottom of a deep layer of air, many kilometres high. It weighs about a kilogram on every square centimetre of the ground.

roots.thread: Air looks like nothing, and yet it fills every gap in a glass of grain, every bottle and every pair of lungs. It keeps moving and mixing round the whole Earth. The oxygen in it was given out by plants and tiny sea beings. You breathe it in, and your breath goes out to be breathed by others, by crows, by the money plant on the window. One invisible air flows through countless separate lives and joins them.

science.text: Air is matter. One litre near the ground weighs about 1.2 grams, and the air above each square centimetre of ground weighs about 1 kilogram.
Almost all the oxygen in the air was made by living things through photosynthesis, building up from about 2,400 million years ago.
How much of today's oxygen is made in the sea, and how much on land, is still being measured. Most estimates say about half comes from the sea.

other_view.view: Air is a mixture of gas particles, and breathing is gases moving in and out of the lungs. Calling the air one breath that joins all lives is a lovely way of speaking, but it adds no new fact about air.

practice.title: Feel the air you cannot see
practice.say: Sit still and close your eyes. Hold your hand a little in front of your mouth. Breathe in slowly through your nose. Notice the cool air going in. Now breathe out slowly through your mouth onto your hand. Notice the warm air coming out. Do this five times. Now open your eyes and look at the room. All of it is full of air, and you are sharing it with everyone here.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, project and challenge was walked through as if at home today, with the materials listed. The Full Glass test was chosen because it needs only two glasses, three grains every kitchen has, water and a ruler, and its result is not obvious: children usually expect big chana to leave much more air than mustard seeds, and the numbers come out close. Glasses are filled to a tape line 2 cm below the rim and tapped so the grains settle, so pouring does not spill. Mustard seeds soak in slowly, so the step says to pour slowly and wait a minute. The grains are not wasted: soak the chana for sundal and sprout the moong. The syringe test uses a syringe with no needle, which any chemist sells, and works over a bowl because water squirts past the finger. The balloon in the bottle needs a 1-litre plastic bottle, and a grown-up makes the hole. The soda test needs a kitchen scale that shows grams; the step gives a football as a second choice and says what to do if the scale shows no change. The lotus activity is marked 'if you can buy lotus stem'. Parents should know: burst balloon pieces can choke small children. The game works for one child alone. Timings were checked step by step. The spine fits about 85 minutes.

how_we_found_out.story: About 2,500 years ago, in ancient Greece, many people thought that a pot with nothing you could see in it was empty. They believed the air inside was nothing at all. The thinker Anaxagoras and his followers showed this was wrong, using things anyone had at home. They blew up a leather wine bag and squeezed it. The bag pushed back, because air was inside. They also used a water thief, a metal jar with small holes in the bottom and a narrow neck at the top. Dip it in water, and water flows in through the holes. But close the top with your thumb first, and hardly any water gets in. The air inside is in the way. Another thinker, Empedocles, described a girl playing with a water thief, and used it to explain breathing. About 500 years later, Hero of Alexandria wrote a book about air. He said that vessels which look empty are full of air. He said air is made of tiny pieces with empty space between them, and that is why it can be squashed.
how_we_found_out.who: Anaxagoras and Empedocles, thinkers in ancient Greece, and later Hero of Alexandria, an engineer in Egypt
how_we_found_out.when: About 450 BCE (the wine bags and the water thief), and the first century CE (Hero's book Pneumatica)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many people thought that a pot holding only air was empty, because air seemed to be nothing. The squeezed wine bags and the water thief showed that air is a real thing that takes up space and pushes back. The philosopher Aristotle wrote about these tests in his book Physics.
